idiom_name: IDisposable + using over the resource; the pool's Return is the explicit hand-back
implementation_notes: Return the resource typed as the narrowest IDisposable the client may release, and let the using statement (or a using declaration) guarantee the hand-back on every exit path; asynchronous resources use IAsyncDisposable with await using. What Dispose means is the owner's decision, not the client's: for borrowed pooled objects the owner exposes its own path - Microsoft.Extensions.ObjectPool documents Get to take an object and Return to give it back, and disposes objects that are never returned - so an API that lends pooled instances wraps Return in the returned type instead of exposing the pool. The classic C++ structure (a smart-pointer type carrying ownership) is replaced by the IDisposable/using convention plus the owner-side policy, and remains justified only when a non-IDisposable legacy handle must be surfaced.
pitfalls: Returning to the pool is not the same as disposing: a wrapper (or a pool policy) that calls Dispose on pooled instances destroys objects the pool intended to reuse; the returned type must own the Return path.
Dispose is expected to be idempotent, so a naive pooled wrapper that returns the object on every Dispose call pushes it into the free list twice.

An interface-typed return value hides the policy - IDisposable says 'release me', not 'return me to X' - so when clients must return to a specific owner, the owner-side wrapper type itself has to be the return type.
Finalizers and the GC never return a pooled object; a finalizer that tries reintroduces non-deterministic release and can run during shutdown when the pool is already gone.
